clue.text: Mob besieging house after it's missing girl's last seen location?

indicators.note: a mob besieging something surrounds it, so the mob's letters go round the rest

parts.note: a mob is a rabble

indicators.note: house comes after it, so its letters follow in the answer

parts.note: the word it, with the 's as a link

explanation.surface: A crowd lays siege to a house in the search for a missing girl, last seen there.
explanation.walkthrough: The missing girl is Alice, last seen going down into Wonderland; the question mark flags the literary twist.
explanation.definitionFit: Alice vanishes underground by following the White Rabbit into its burrow, so its entrance is where she was last seen.

clue.text: "Midnight shakes the memory / As a madman shakes a dead geranium" (- on a Windy Night, TS Eliot)

definitions.text: "Midnight shakes the memory / As a madman shakes a dead geranium" (- on a Windy Night, TS Eliot)

parts.words: "Midnight shakes the memory / As a madman shakes a dead geranium" (- on a Windy Night, TS Eliot)
parts.note: a quotation clue: the dash stands for the missing first word of the title of the Eliot poem these lines come from

explanation.definitionFit: The lines open the second stanza of an early TS Eliot poem whose title begins with this word, a free-ranging musical composition.

clue.text: Part of score by Britten arranged with wrong lyricist

parts.note: a bar is one measured section of a musical score

indicators.note: arranged suits music: the letters are set out in a new order

parts.note: taken as written
taken as written

explanation.surface: A section of a Britten score has been set out with the wrong words by its librettist.
explanation.walkthrough: 'wrong' looks like a second anagram signal but its letters are needed: BAR, BRITTEN and WRONG give fifteen letters, rearranged by 'arranged'.
explanation.definitionFit: Elizabeth, the Victorian poet of Sonnets from the Portuguese, wrote lyric verse, so she can be called a lyricist.

clue.text: Small diagram head of editorial's put in this month

indicators.note: the editorial's head letter is put into the other piece, so it goes inside

parts.note: INST, short for instant, is old business-letter usage for this month

indicators.note: the head of a word is its first letter

explanation.surface: A little chart at the top of the editorial is going in this month's issue.
explanation.walkthrough: INST is the old commercial abbreviation for 'instant', meaning this month; E goes inside it.
explanation.definitionFit: A small map or picture set into a corner of a larger one is an inset.

clue.text: Accept Shakespearean villain not principally a kind of hero

parts.note: to have something is to accept it

indicators.note: principally points to the first letter, which is removed from the villain

parts.note: Iago is the villain of Othello

explanation.surface: Someone agrees that a Shakespearean villain is not, at heart, any sort of hero.
explanation.walkthrough: A HAVE-A-GO hero is a British phrase for a member of the public who tackles a criminal.
explanation.definitionFit: The phrase names an ordinary bystander praised for confronting a robber or thug, a particular sort of brave citizen.

clue.text: Broken tub blocks Missy and Dexter's way to Woodstock

indicators.note: the broken tub blocks the girl, sitting in her middle

parts.note: missy and lass are both words for a girl

indicators.note: the letters of tub are broken up and rearranged

explanation.surface: A broken bath gets in the way of two people heading for the 1969 Woodstock festival.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Broken' makes STBU, which 'blocks' puts inside LASS. Missy and Dexter look like a pair of travellers; Dexter is Colin Dexter, whose first Inspector Morse novel is Last Bus to Woodstock.
explanation.definitionFit: Colin Dexter's first Morse mystery takes its title from the late-night service to Woodstock, near Oxford.

clue.text: Halt academic pursuits other than arts and humanities

definitions.meaning: to halt a flow is to stop it, as in stopping bleeding

definitions.text: academic pursuits other than arts and humanities
definitions.meaning: science, technology, engineering and mathematics, known by their initials

explanation.surface: Someone calls for a stop to every subject that is not an arts or humanities course.
explanation.definitionFit: To stem a tide is to check it; the acronym groups the sciences, technology, engineering and maths.

clue.text: Fancy Moleskine notebook now regularly used for play that Will helped write

indicators.note: fancy as an adjective means elaborate, so the letters are worked into a new pattern

parts.note: taken as written

indicators.note: regularly means every other letter, here the first, third and so on

explanation.surface: An elegant brand notebook is now regularly used for drafting a play Shakespeare co-wrote.
explanation.walkthrough: Alternate letters of 'notebook now' give NTBONW; with MOLESKINE these fifteen letters are rearranged. Will is Shakespeare, who wrote the play with John Fletcher.
explanation.definitionFit: This late tragicomedy, based on Chaucer's Knight's Tale, is a joint work of Shakespeare and Fletcher.

clue.text: It's said I love company work located in Colorado

definitions.meaning: the proverb says that wretchedness loves company, so the clue speaks as that unhappy state
the Stephen King novel set in a remote Colorado farmhouse

explanation.surface: Someone announces they love company and works in Colorado.
explanation.definitionFit: The proverb runs that unhappiness likes others to share it; Stephen King's novel of a captive writer takes place in the Colorado Rockies.

clue.text: Trouble's most of what follows Paddy Clarke after university, alongside brother

indicators.note: the laughter comes after the university letter in the answer
most of means the last part is cut off

parts.note: Roddy Doyle's Booker-winning novel is Paddy Clarke Ha Ha Ha

explanation.surface: Most of a Roddy Doyle novel's title comes after a student's sibling gets into trouble.
explanation.definitionFit: A brouhaha is a noisy fuss or commotion, the sort of trouble that draws a crowd.

clue.text: As a verb is changed they might add polish

indicators.note: changed tells us the preceding letters are put into a different order

explanation.surface: A grammar lesson: when a verb changes form, it adds a little polish.
explanation.walkthrough: 'is' is part of the fodder, not a link: AS A VERB IS gives the nine letters.
explanation.definitionFit: Sandpaper and scouring powders are rubbed on surfaces to smooth and shine them.

clue.text: More than one course discussed novel dealing with slavery

indicators.note: discussed means spoken about, so we want a word sounding like the courses

parts.note: courses taken on a journey are routes

explanation.surface: Several courses were discussed, including a novel about slavery.
explanation.walkthrough: 'course' suggests a menu or a class, but it is a route.
explanation.definitionFit: Alex Haley's novel traces an African American family from Kunta Kinte, enslaved in Gambia, through generations of slavery.

clue.text: Bob Marley perhaps, and second of Wailers ranges

indicators.note: to bob is to cut short, so the last letter is docked

parts.note: Jacob Marley appears to Scrooge as a ghost, or spectre, in A Christmas Carol

indicators.note: second of means the second letter of the word that follows

explanation.surface: Bob Marley and the Wailers, it seems, have a wide range.
explanation.walkthrough: Bob Marley reads as the reggae singer, with the Wailers his band; but 'Bob' means cut short, and Marley is Scrooge's ghostly partner.
explanation.definitionFit: Spectra are full ranges, as in a spectrum of opinion or of colours.

clue.text: Book city pair returned: A Room of One's Own? polonius

indicators.note: returned means sent back, so the city and the pair are read backwards together

parts.note: Rio de Janeiro, often just Rio
a duo is a pair

explanation.surface: A book about a city twinning: is it Virginia Woolf's A Room of One's Own?
explanation.walkthrough: The trailing word 'polonius' and the missing enumeration look like a print slip, perhaps from the setter's name Apollonius; it plays no part in the parse.
explanation.definitionFit: A lady's private sitting room or bedroom is a place she has entirely to herself.

clue.text: School party is sure to entertain our son

indicators.note: to entertain a guest is to take them in, so the son goes inside

parts.note: a do is a party
shall expresses certainty, as in 'you shall go to the ball'
parents speak of their son as the boy

explanation.surface: A school party is sure to welcome our son.
explanation.walkthrough: The school is Wackford Squeers's brutal academy in Dickens's Nicholas Nickleby.
explanation.definitionFit: Dickens's Yorkshire boarding establishment run by Squeers is the most notorious fictional school in English literature.

clue.text: Approves of intention to replace lead character of Equus?

indicators.note: the first letter of the word is swapped for another piece

parts.note: Equus is the Latin name for the horse genus; the question mark allows the plural
an end is an aim or intention

explanation.surface: Someone backs the plan to recast the leading role in Peter Shaffer's play Equus.
explanation.walkthrough: 'lead character' suggests the boy in Shaffer's play, but it is just the first letter.
explanation.definitionFit: To endorse something is to give it your backing or approval.

clue.text: Plants who took in member of pirate's' operations

parts.words: who took in member of pirate's'
parts.note: in Peter Pan the crocodile swallowed Captain Hook's hand, a member of the pirate
uses are workings or operations

explanation.surface: Some plants were being used by a person who took in a member of a pirate crew.
explanation.walkthrough: The 'member' is Hook's severed hand, eaten by the crocodile that ticks after him.
explanation.definitionFit: These spring-flowering bulbs, often purple or yellow, are garden plants.

clue.text: Rich vigilante's' enemy has broken key law in Hoban's dystopian tale

indicators.note: the enemy has the broken letters within him

parts.note: Batman, the rich vigilante Bruce Wayne, has the Riddler as an enemy

indicators.note: broken means the letters are smashed and reassembled

explanation.surface: A wealthy vigilante's foe has broken a key law in Russell Hoban's novel.
explanation.walkthrough: 'broken' turns KEY LAW into YWALKE, which goes inside RIDDLER before its last letter.
explanation.definitionFit: Russell Hoban's 1980 novel is set in a post-nuclear Kent and narrated in a decayed English.

clue.text: Expose "first in literature" by comic poet not finishing claimed degree

indicators.note: first in means the opening letter of the word
the poet claims the degree, taking it inside
not finishing means the last letter is dropped

parts.note: Pam Ayres is a popular English writer of comic verse
BA, a Bachelor of Arts, is a university degree

explanation.surface: A comic poet who never graduated is exposed as having lied about a literature first.
explanation.walkthrough: Pam AYRES is a well-known British comic poet; losing her last letter she becomes AYRE, which holds BA.
explanation.definitionFit: To lay something bare is to uncover or reveal it.

clue.text: In the end, Cardinal Wolsey's strange old paper does this

indicators.note: strange signals that the letters come out in an odd order
in the end means the last letter of the word

parts.note: Wolsey, with the 's as a link

explanation.surface: Cardinal Wolsey's strange old papers end up in an archive.
explanation.walkthrough: 'strange' rearranges L and WOLSEY.
explanation.definitionFit: Ageing paper turns a pale amber colour, which is what old newsprint does.

clue.text: Host a new struggling writer

parts.note: MC, master of ceremonies, is a host

indicators.note: struggling letters thrash about into a new order

explanation.surface: A struggling writer is hosting a new event.
explanation.walkthrough: 'struggling writer' wants to be one phrase, but 'struggling' is the anagram signal and Ian McEwan is a very successful novelist.
explanation.definitionFit: Ian McEwan is the English novelist of Atonement and Amsterdam.

clue.text: Dictionary writer's word superficially adopted by Booker winner Peter

indicators.note: adopted by means taken in by the novelist's name

parts.note: Peter Carey won the Booker Prize twice

indicators.note: superficially means only on the surface, the first and last letters

explanation.surface: A Booker-winning novelist borrows a lexicographer's word without going deep.
explanation.walkthrough: Robert Cawdrey compiled the first English dictionary, A Table Alphabeticall (1604).
explanation.definitionFit: Cawdrey's 1604 word list was the first monolingual English dictionary.

clue.text: Spartan clan somehow including Odysseus, initially in charge

indicators.note: the shuffled clan includes the hero's letter inside it
somehow means arranged in some way or other
initially means the first letter

explanation.surface: A Spartan clan somehow takes in Odysseus to lead it.
explanation.walkthrough: 'somehow' turns CLAN into LACN, which includes O. Laconia was the region around Sparta.
explanation.definitionFit: Spartans, from Laconia, were famous for terse speech, so spartan and laconic both mean brief.

clue.text: Book one's stopped to edit for length

indicators.note: a stopped bottle has something in its neck, so these go inside

explanation.definitionFit: The cubit was an ancient measure of length from elbow to fingertip.

clue.text: Creator of web text content of new hit e-zine

explanation.definitionFit: EB White wrote Charlotte's Web, the children's book about a spider.

clue.text: Deathly devices from opening of Arundel Tomb, and some more after the opening

parts.note: taken as written

indicators.note: after the opening means with the first letter gone

parts.note: some more tombs, the word made plural

explanation.walkthrough: An Arundel Tomb is Larkin's poem; 'some more' gives TOMBS, beheaded by 'after the opening'.
